const { return {x * s, y * s, z * s}; }\n    Vec3 operator/(val_t s) const { return {x / s, y / s, z / s}; }\n    Vec3 operator-() const { return {-x, -y, -z}; }\n\n    val_t dot(const Vec3& o) const { return x * o.x + y * o.y + z * o.z; }\n    Vec3 cross(const Vec3& o) const {\n        return {y * o.z - z * o.y, z * o.x - x * o.z, x * o.y - y * o.x};\n    }\n\n    val_t squaredNorm() const { return x * x + y * y + z * z; }\n    val_t norm() const { return std::sqrt(squaredNorm()); }\n    Vec3 normalized() const {\n        val_t n = norm();\n        return n > EPSILON ? *this / n : Vec3();\n    }\n\n    bool operator==(const Vec3& o) const {\n        return std::abs(x - o.x) < EPSILON && std::abs(y - o.y) < EPSILON && std::abs(z - o.z) < EPSILON;\n    }\n};\n\nstruct Triangle {}\n\n    Vec3 center() const { return (a + b + c) / 3.0f; }\n    Vec3 normal() const { return _normal; }\n\n    val_t area() const {\n        Vec3 ab = b - a;\n        Vec3 ac = c - a;\n edges\n    Vec3 e0 = v1 - v0;\n    Vec3 e1 = v2 - v1;\n    Vec3 e2 = v0 - v2;\n\n    // Test box normals (AABB axes)\n    auto minMax3 = [](val_t a, val_t b, val_t c) {\n        return std::make_pair(std::min({a, b, c}), std::max({a, b, c}));\n    };\n\n    auto [minX, maxX] = minMax3(v0.x, v1.x, v2.x);\n    if (minX > boxHalfSize.x || maxX < -boxHalfSize.x) return false;\n\n    auto [minY, maxY] = minMax3(v0.y, v1.y, v2.y);\n    if (minY > boxHalfSize.y || maxY < -boxHalfSize.y) return false;\n\n    auto [minZ, maxZ] = minMax3(v0.z, v1.z, v2.z);\n    if (minZ > boxHalfSize.z boxHalfSize.y * std::abs(axis.y) +\n                  boxHalfSize.z * std::abs(axis.z);\n        auto [minP, maxP] = minMax3(p0, p1, p2);\n        return !(minP > r || maxP < -r);\n    };\n\n    Vec3 axes[3] = {{1,0,0}, {0,1,0}, {0,0,1}};\n    Vec3 edges[3] = {e0, e1, e2};\n    for (const auto& axis : axes) {\n        for (const auto& edge : edges) {\n            Vec3 crossAxis = std::max(maxBound.z, v->z);\n            }\n        }\n\n        // Collect all indices\n        std::vector<size_t> allIndices(triangles.size());\n        for (size_t i = 0; i < triangles.size();      minBound = nodeMin;\n        maxBound = nodeMax;\n        halfExtent = (maxBound - minBound) * 0.5f;\n        center = (minBound + maxBound) * 0.5f;\n\n        // If few enough triangles or too return;\n        }\n\n        // Subdivide into 8 children\n        Vec3 childHalfSize = halfExtent * 0.5f;\n        std::vector<size_t> childIndices[8];\n\n        for (size_t idx : indices) {\n            const Triangle& tri = (*allTriangles)[idx];\n\n            // Check which children this triangle overlaps\n            for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i) {\n                Vec3 childCenter = center;\n                childCenter.x += (i & 1) ? childHalfSize.x : -childHalfSize.x;\n                childCenter.y += (i & 2) ? childHalfSize.y : -childHalfSize.y;\n                childCenter.z += (i & 4) ? childHalfSize.z : -childHalfSize.z;\n\n                if (triangleBoxOverlap(childCenter, childHalfSize, tri)) {\n                    childIndices[i].push_back(idx);\n                }\n            }\n        }\n\n        // Check if we can't split further (all triangles in one child)\n        bool canSplit = false;\n        for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i) {\n            if (!childIndices[i].empty() && childIndices[i].size() < indices.size()) {\n                canSplit = true;\n                break;\n            }\n        }\n\n        if (!canSplit) {\n            triangleIndices = indices;\n            return;\n        }\n\n        // Build children\n        for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i) {\n            if (!childIndices[i].empty()) {\n                Vec3 childMin = center;\n                Vec3 childMax = center;\n                childMin.x = (i & 1) ? center.x : minBound.x;\n                childMax.x = (i & 1) ? maxBound.x : center.x;\n                childMin.y = (i & 2) ? center.y : minBound.y;\n                childMax.y = (i & 2) ? maxBound.y : center.y;\n                childMin.z = (i & 4) ? center.z : minBound.z;\n                childMax.z = (i & 4) ? maxBound.z : (std::abs(c.y) > halfExtent.y + ad.y) return false;\n        if (std::abs(c.z) > halfExtent.z + ad.z) return false;\n\n        if (std::abs(d.y * c.z - d.z * c.y) > halfExtent.y * ad.z + halfExtent.z {"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1792986939710,"sessionID":"ses_e89a8dbd3ffeuAMQyA8X5vGawy","part":{"id":"prt_176574a24001mTGFFwljIl5Uf7","messageID":"msg_1765744260010oI9PY3aA1Gl1m","sessionID":"ses_e89a8dbd3ffeuAMQyA8X5vGawy","type":"reasoning","text":"I'm realizing the form-factor computation relies on a single sequential RNG stream across all pairs, so parallelizing on GPU would break exact output equivalence unless I use per-pair skip-ahead in the mt19937 sequence to reproduce identical results.\n\nStoring the full random stream explodes in memory for large triangle counts, and replicating Mersenne Twister jump-ahead on the GPU would require implementing matrix-based state advancement, which is heavy engineering. I'm now questioning whether bit-identical reproducibility is even required, or whether matching the statistical/aggregate result is sufficient.\n\nGiven that fragility, I'll aim to match the RNG stream exactly and verify against the original's hash, documenting any divergence if it occurs. For the wave simulation, I can parallelize over i per timestep since each i is independent and the inner j-reduction stays sequential per thread, while timesteps remain strictly sequential since each depends on the prior one—with N=5120 and T=50 that's about 1.3e9 operations, well within GPU capacity.\n\nThe j-loop is memory-bound and strided across threads, so transposing tau and kij to column-major layout would make reads coalesced across i while still preserving the sequential summation order needed for exact float matching. For the distance computation, I can parallelize the correlation calculation across all (i,t) pairs since each inner sum over tt stays sequential, then do a strict sequential argmax per i afterward to preserve exact tie-breaking behavior.\n\nFor form factors, I'd parallelize over the N*N pairs and flatten the octree into arrays (bounds, child indices, triangle ranges) with an explicit fixed-depth stack for GPU traversal, since the blocking test is a pure boolean predicate and order-independent. The harder problem is RNG determinism — I'm weighing whether to accept a different random stream via a GPU-friendly generator like Philox, or try to exactly replicate the Mersenne Twister sequence through jump-ahead, since everything else (normal culling, traversal) is deterministic but the per-pair ray sampling offset depends on exact stream position.\n\nTracing through libstdc++'s uniform_real_distribution implementation, I confirm each call draws exactly one 32-bit MT output, so each pair consumes 64 draws regardless of occlusion outcome, and the offset for a given pair is 64 times the count of valid prior pairs. Reproducing this exactly would mean computing the MT state at an arbitrary draw index, which requires jump-ahead math rather than just iterating the generator.\n\nBut storing the full stream is infeasible at scale—for N=5120 that's already 6.7GB, and larger N makes it worse. A chunked approach where the host generates MT outputs sequentially in bounded batches and streams them to the GPU would be exact and memory-safe, though the host-side generation time (a few seconds for ~1.7e9 numbers) plus PCIe transfer could become the bottleneck compared to GPU-side form factor computation with octree-accelerated ray casting. I'm now considering whether generating the MT sequence directly on GPU by having threads start from checkpointed states would be a better alternative.\n\nParallelizing MT generation itself is tricky because each 624-word block has internal dependencies through the twist recurrence, requiring the twist to be computed in phases within a block—this is getting complicated enough that I'm questioning whether it's worth it versus just doing the jump-ahead polynomial trick, which also carries its own complexity.\n\nEven with double-buffered host-side MT generation overlapped against GPU compute, I'm still bound by host generation throughput for large N, which undercuts true scalability. The alternative—a Philox-based per-pair RNG fully on GPU—would scale cleanly but changes the numerical output since the hash values and resulting distances wouldn't match the original benchmark.\n\nGiven the \"equivalent semantics\" requirement likely means matching the original random stream exactly, I'm leaning toward keeping the host-generated MT19937 stream overlapped with GPU work rather than switching RNG schemes, even though a fully parallel block-wise twist on GPU would be ideal if it weren't so complex to synchronize correctly.\n\nBut this only parallelizes within one block of 624 outputs — generating the full 1.7e9-length stream still means looping sequentially over roughly 2.7 million blocks, each requiring several syncs, which adds up to real overhead despite the per-block parallelism.\n\nThen I consider jumping the RNG state ahead via polynomial jump-ahead so the GPU can generate independent chunks starting from arbitrary offsets, but computing a jump-ahead state for Mersenne Twister requires heavy polynomial arithmetic (roughly 19937²/64 operations) per jump, which is too costly to do per-pair. Doing it per chunk of say 1024 pairs is more reasonable, but each chunk still needs 65536 sequential draws internally, so I'm weighing how to parallelize that inner generation too.\n\nGiven the difficulty, I decide to just accept the host-generated stream approach and optimize it: std::mt19937 can emit roughly one output per 1.5ns at -O3, so 1.7 billion draws would take about 2.5 seconds, plus pinned-memory transfer of ~6.7GB at 20GB/s adds another 0.3s — manageable with double buffering so the host fills the next chunk while the GPU processes the current one. I also note the grader's default test size (320 triangles) is trivial, and even larger sizes like 1280 or 5120 should be fine, so I settle on this approach, trusting that matching the original's hash output exactly is the best verification method, while also flagging floating-point determinism concerns between GPU and CPU math operations.\n\nBoth nvcc and GCC by default enable FMA contraction (nvcc via --fmad=true, GCC via -ffp-contract=fast under C++20/gnu++20 with -march=native), so sqrt and division should be IEEE-compliant and correctly rounded on both sides, but FMA contraction patterns may not match exactly between host and device code, risking subtle bit-level mismatches. I can't selectively disable contraction on just one side without altering the original binary's behavior, so I decide to test empirically first and only add compiler flags like -ffp-contract=off if the hashes don't align, since modifying build flags (not the executable name) should still be within the rules.\n\nFor the CUDA integration itself, I'm keeping roomsim.cpp unrenamed but using CMake's `set_source_files_properties` with `LANGUAGE CUDA` so nvcc compiles it directly without creating new files, and I need to make sure -march=native gets passed through via -Xcompiler so nvcc forwards it correctly to the host compiler.\n\nNow I'm walking through porting the simulation pipeline to GPU: icosphere generation and octree construction stay on CPU since they're cheap at this scale, while the O(N²) time-delay computation gets parallelized on the device. I need to make sure the distance and ceiling calculations replicate the exact floating-point expression order from the CPU version so results match, particularly around the squared-norm computation and potential FMA contraction differences.\n\nI'm resolving the FMA mismatch concern by deciding to disable floating-point contraction on both host and device (`-ffp-contract=off` and `--fmad=false`), ensuring both sides use strict separate IEEE operations and produce identical results.\n\nFor comparing outputs, I'll build the original binary first and record its results before changing flags, since the host path is being replaced entirely by the GPU path but still handles mesh generation, octree construction, RNG streams, and printing. Then I'm turning to the form factor computation kernel design — a per-pair GPU kernel taking triangle data, the flattened octree, and RNG stream chunks, producing the N×N kij matrix while tracking culling and offset mapping for random draws per pair.\n\nI'm weighing whether to compute the exclusive prefix count of valid (non-culled) pairs on host versus GPU, avoiding CUB or thrust to keep dependencies minimal — settling on a row-counting GPU kernel followed by a host-side exclusive scan over per-row totals, with each row's internal offsets computed sequentially within its own thread.\n\nBut that raises the problem of coordinating RNG draws: since the host needs chunk draw counts before generating the random stream, I'd run the counting kernel first, copy counts back, compute prefix offsets per chunk, then generate draws for that chunk — but assigning per-pair offsets within a row still forces one thread per row, which gives poor occupancy for small N.\n\nActually for realistic N (like 5120, giving ~2.6e7 pairs and ~4e8 ray casts), one-thread-per-row is far too little parallelism — I need thread-per-pair instead, which means computing draw offsets via a GPU-wide exclusive scan over all N² pair flags rather than per-row serial prefixes.\n\nSimpler plan: a pass-1 kernel marks valid pairs as flags, then I run an exclusive scan over the flattened array to get the compacted offsets directly, avoiding the awkward per-row shared-memory scan approach.\n\nActually, I realize I could just compute the offsets on the host instead — looping over the N² pairs with the same cull test takes only tens of milliseconds, which is cheap enough, as long as the host's dot-product cull decision exactly matches what the device will compute so the offsets line up correctly.\n\nPer-row chunking would change the stream mapping and break the hash, so that's out. Instead I'll chunk by row ranges, having the host compute relative offsets and valid flags within each chunk, generate the needed MT outputs into a pinned buffer sized for that chunk, and copy them over incrementally.\n\nThe GPU kernel then just reads each pair's chunk-relative offset and flag to pick up its draws. Since host-side MT generation dominates the cost (~1.7e9 draws, a couple seconds) and GPU octree traversal for form factors is similarly a second or two, overlapping them with double buffering should get total runtime down to roughly 2-3 seconds versus the original 100+ second CPU approach -- good enough, and I'll be upfront about the tradeoffs when reporting results.\n\nI keep circling back to whether the host RNG bottleneck can be parallelized -- jump-ahead polynomials for MT19937 exist in theory but implementing them is overkill here, and precomputing per-block states just reduces to sequential generation anyway. The RNG itself stays as one persistent std::mt19937 generating draws continuously across chunks, feeding into a uniform_real_distribution for the actual random values.\n\nTo match libstdc++'s exact output I need to replicate how generate_canonical builds a float from raw engine outputs -- accumulating weighted draws into a sum and normalizing -- then how uniform_real_distribution scales that canonical value into the target range.\n\nI'm working out the exact arithmetic: dividing by the sum and clamping with nextafter if it hits 1, then scaling by the range width. This means the result is just the uint32 converted to float, scaled by 2^-32, with nextafter clamping if it rounds up to 1.0 -- and I want to replicate this precisely on the device so results match the host-side distribution bit for bit.\n\nI'm now tracing the order of random draws per ray: picking a point in the first triangle consumes two random values (u, v), then the second triangle consumes two more, giving four floats per ray pair and sixty-four per batch of sixteen pairs, with the reflection adjustment applied when u+v exceeds 1 but without skipping any RNG draws.\n\nI need to be careful about floating-point contraction (FMA) in the triangle point evaluation, since that could subtly change results between host and device, so I'll check the disassembly for fused multiply-add instructions before deciding on a policy.\n\nNow I'm working through the octree's flattened node structure on the device, examining how leaf versus non-leaf nodes are distinguished by whether their triangle index list is empty, and flagging a potential edge case where a leaf could technically have zero triangles.\n\nI'm also noting that the root node itself skips the bounding-box intersection check during traversal — only its children get box-tested — and reasoning that since the final result is just a boolean of whether any triangle blocks the ray, I only need to replicate the exact same traversal order and visited leaves to preserve correctness.\n\nSince a triangle could appear in multiple leaves but the function short-circuits on the first block found, duplicates don't affect the boolean outcome. Wave propagation using radiosity equations with time delays (Tau)\n * 3. Distance estimation via cross-correlation of radiosity values\n * \n * The implementation generates a procedural icosphere mesh to simulate a room.\n *\n * GPU parallelization:\n *  - Tau and Kij are computed with one CUDA thread per (receiver, emitter) pair.\n *  - Kij ray casting traverses a flattened octree on the device.\n *  - The random stream for Kij is the exact sequential std::mt19937(42) stream of the\n *    original code. The host generates it in row-major pair order (culled pairs consume\n *    no numbers) in chunks, overlapped with device execution, so results are identical.\n *  - Wave propagation is parallel over receivers per timestep. Timesteps remain\n *    sequential (true data dependency). Each receiver's sum over emitters keeps the\n *    original summation order, so results are bit-identical.\n *  - Cross-correlation is parallel over (lag, triangle), followed by a per-triangle argmax.\n */\n\n#include <algorithm>\n#include <array>\n#include <chrono>\n#include <cmath>\n#include <cstdint>\n#include <cstdio>\n#include <cstdlib>\n#include <cstring>\n#include <limits>\n#include <map>\n#include <memory>\n#include <random>\n#include <utility>\n#include <vector>\n\n#include <cuda_runtime.h>\n\n#include \"../common/results_output.hpp\"\n\n#define HD __host__ __device__\n\n#define CUDA_CHECK(call)                                                          \\\n    do {                                                                          \\\n        cudaError_t err_ = (call);                                                \\\n        if (err_ != cudaSuccess) {                                                \\\n            fprintf(stderr, \"CUDA error at %s:%d: %s\\n\", __FILE__, __LINE__,      \\\n                    cudaGetErrorString(err_));                                    \\\n            exit(EXIT_FAILURE);                                                   \\\n        }                                                                         \\\n    } while (0)\n\n// ============================================================================\n// Types and Constants\n// ============================================================================\n\nusing idx_t = uint32_t;\nusing val_t = float;\n\nconstexpr val_t PI = 3.14159265358979323846f;\nconstexpr val_t ZERO = 0.0f;\nconstexpr val_t ONE = 1.0f;\nconstexpr val_t WAVE_SPEED = 0.5f;        // Wave propagation speed (units per timestep)\nconstexpr val_t INV_WAVE_SPEED = 1.0f / WAVE_SPEED;\nconstexpr int NUM_RAYS = 16;              // Number of rays for visibility sampling\nconstexpr val_t INV_NUM_RAYS = 1.0f / NUM_RAYS;\nconstexpr val_t EPSILON = 1e-6f;\nconstexpr val_t VAL_MAX = 3.402823466e+38f;   // std::numeric_limits<float>::max()\n\nconstexpr int THREADS_PER_BLOCK = 256;\n\n// Host/device min/max with the exact semantics of std::min / std::max.\nHD inline val_t vmin(val_t a, val_t b) { return b < a ? b : a; }\nHD inline val_t vmax(val_t a, val_t b) { return a < b ? b : a; }\nHD inline val_t vabs(val_t x) { return fabsf(x); }\n\n// ============================================================================\n// Vector and Triangle Types\n// ============================================================================\n\nstruct Vec3 {\n    val_t x, y, z;\n\n    HD constexpr Vec3() : x(0), y(0), z(0) {}\n    HD constexpr Vec3(val_t x, val_t y, val_t z) : x(x), y(y), z(z) {}\n    HD explicit constexpr Vec3(val_t v) : x(v), y(v), z(v) {}\n\n    HD Vec3 operator+(const Vec3& o) const { return {x + o.x, y + o.y, z + o.z}; }\n    HD Vec3 operator-(const Vec3& o) const { return {x - o.x, y - o.y, z - o.z}; }\n    HD Vec3 operator*(val_t s) const { return {x * s, y * s, z * s}; }\n    HD Vec3 operator/(val_t s) const { return {x / s, y / s, z / s}; }\n    HD Vec3 operator-() const { return {-x, -y, -z}; }\n\n    HD val_t dot(const Vec3& o) const { return x * o.x + y * o.y + z * o.z; }\n    HD Vec3 cross(const Vec3& o) const {\n        return {y * o.z - z * o.y, z * o.x - x * o.z, x * o.y - y * o.x};\n    }\n\n    HD val_t squaredNorm() const { return x * x + y * y + z * z; }\n    HD val_t norm() const { return sqrtf(squaredNorm()); }\n    HD Vec3 normalized() const {\n        val_t n = norm();\n        return n > EPSILON ? *this / n : Vec3();\n    }\n\n    bool operator==(const Vec3& o) const {\n        return std::abs(x - o.x) < EPSILON && std::abs(y - o.y) < EPSILON && std::abs(z - o.z) < EPSILON;\n    }\n};\n\nstruct Triangle {\n    Vec3 a, b, c;\n    Vec3 _normal;\n\n    Triangle() = default;\n    Triangle(const Vec3& a, const Vec3& b, const Vec3& c)\n        : a(a), b(b), c(c), _normal((b - a).cross(c - a).normalized()) {}\n\n    HD Vec3 center() const { return (a + b + c) / 3.0f; }\n    HD Vec3 normal() const { return _normal; }\n\n    val_t area() const {\n        Vec3 ab = b - a;\n        Vec3 ac = c - a;\n        return 0.5f * ab.cross(ac).norm();\n    }\n\n    bool operator==(const Triangle& o) const { return a == o.a && b == o.b && c == o.c; }\n};\n\n// ============================================================================\n// Triangle-Box Overlap Test (for octree construction)\n// ============================================================================\n\n// Separating axis test for triangle-box overlap\nbool triangleBoxOverlap(const Vec3& boxCenter, const Vec3& boxHalfSize, const Triangle& tri) {\n    // Translate triangle to box center\n    Vec3 v0 = tri.a - boxCenter;\n    Vec3 v1 = tri.b - boxCenter;\n    Vec3 v2 = tri.c - boxCenter;\n\n    // Triangle edges\n    Vec3 e0 = v1 - v0;\n    Vec3 e1 = v2 - v1;\n    Vec3 e2 = v0 - v2;\n\n    // Test box normals (AABB axes)\n    auto minMax3 = [](val_t a, val_t b, val_t c) {\n        return std::make_pair(std::min({a, b, c}), std::max({a, b, c}));\n    };\n\n    auto [minX, maxX] = minMax3(v0.x, v1.x, v2.x);\n    if (minX > boxHalfSize.x || maxX < -boxHalfSize.x) return false;\n\n    auto [minY, maxY] = minMax3(v0.y, v1.y, v2.y);\n    if (minY > boxHalfSize.y || maxY < -boxHalfSize.y) return false;\n\n    auto [minZ, maxZ] = minMax3(v0.z, v1.z, v2.z);\n    if (minZ > boxHalfSize.z || maxZ < -boxHalfSize.z) return false;\n\n    // Test triangle normal\n    Vec3 triNormal = e0.cross(e1);\n    val_t d = triNormal.dot(v0);\n    val_t r = boxHalfSize.x * std::abs(triNormal.x) +\n              boxHalfSize.y * std::abs(triNormal.y) +\n              boxHalfSize.z * std::abs(triNormal.z);\n    if (std::abs(d) > r) return false;\n\n    // Test 9 edge cross products\n    auto testAxis = [&](const Vec3& axis) {\n        val_t p0 = axis.dot(v0);\n        val_t p1 = axis.dot(v1);\n        val_t p2 = axis.dot(v2);\n        val_t r = boxHalfSize.x * std::abs(axis.x) +\n {"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1792987732069,"sessionID":"ses_e89a8dbd3ffeuAMQyA8X5vGawy","part":{"id":"prt_176655281001JUbox7Y3LGJ8cI","messageID":"msg_176654e3e001EANF57YAvk5BHp","sessionID":"ses_e89a8dbd3ffeuAMQyA8X5vGawy","type":"reasoning","text":"The raw Mersenne Twister generation at 4 seconds for 1.7 billion numbers seems to be the real bottleneck since it's scalar rather than vectorized, with the distribution adding extra overhead on top. I'm now considering parallelizing across the host's 256 cores using jump-ahead techniques to compute MT states at many block positions simultaneously.\n\nLooking into the math, this jump-ahead approach relies on the MT state transition being linear over GF(2), so computing the state after n steps means applying a polynomial reduction of x^n modulo the characteristic polynomial of degree 19937. But estimating the cost, each jump requires around 31 squaring operations with each squaring costing roughly 6 million word operations, and I'd need many such jumps for all the thread starting positions — this is turning out to be far more expensive than it's worth for this use case.\n\nI'm weighing whether the jump-ahead complexity is actually worth it given the risk of subtle bugs versus the performance payoff — maybe 6 seconds versus minutes, but verifiable by hash matching either way. I'm looking for a simpler middle-ground: could I parallelize MT stream generation across host threads without full jump-polynomial machinery, or offload the twist to GPU with block-level parallelism and per-chunk jumps instead.\n\nRealizing the twist itself is cheap and not dependency-bound, so the real bottleneck for parallel scaling is lack of jump-ahead — there's no way around needing it to split work across blocks. Without recalling MT19937's characteristic polynomial directly, I could derive it via Berlekamp-Massey applied to a bitstream from the linear recurrence, which is standard and tractable with bit-packing to keep the operation count reasonable.\n\nBut then implementing the actual jump via polynomial evaluation using Horner's method over the transition operator adds significant complexity, especially since the 624-word state doesn't map cleanly onto the 19937-dimensional transition space — this would require careful handling of the unused seed bits and could balloon into hundreds of lines of fragile code for a benefit that's already dwarfed by the speedup we've gotten. I'm now considering whether a simpler optimization — just cutting per-number overhead — might be a better use of effort than chasing full jump-ahead.\n\nSwitching to generating raw uint32 values instead of going through the distribution layer should shave off a couple seconds by doing the float conversion directly on the GPU, while still matching the reference output exactly. I'll keep host-side RNG generation as the main serial bottleneck but note it rather than attempt full jump-ahead parallelization, since correctness and equivalence matter more than squeezing out that last bit of performance here.\n\nThat clamp matches libstdc++'s generate_canonical behavior exactly, confirming the conversion logic. Now I'm switching the buffers to raw uint32 throughout, adding a nextU32 accessor to the RNG wrapper, and trimming out the now-unused distribution-based rand method to keep things clean.\n\n","time":{"start":1792987714177,"end":1792987732009},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

The distribution adds roughly 2 s on top of that. Since the float conversion is exact (verified above: `float(u) * 2^-32`, clamped to `nextafter(1,0)`), I can move it to the GPU and have the host stage raw 32-bit words. That removes host work without changing any values.\n\nBreaking jump-ahead MT19937 for parallel host generation would be a much larger change to keep the stream exact, so I'll stop at this step.","time":{"start":1792987732014,"end":1792987732027}}}
